messages.subject: INLA coast Boundary mesh problem
messages.subject_clean: INLA coast Boundary mesh problem
messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,
My name is Morgane. I am a PhD student from the University of Aberdeen. I am building an INLA Spatio-temporal log-Gaussian Cox Processes model to assess the distribution of birds in the Firth of Forth area.I am having problems building the INLA mesh. I am trying to build my mesh by point locations(long and lat) and point id numbers from the data_df.txt file.I am also using the FOF_bound_sf file which is the shapefile of the coastal boundary called Coast_FVCOM_bound_shapefile.shp for my mesh. I attached and plotted the data in the zip file. Plot_1, shows the red dots which are the locations of the points to create the mesh triangles inside the FOF_bound_sf. In Plot_2, I am creating the mesh using inla. mesh.create () function, but the mesh seems to be outside my FOF_bound_sf and not inside. In detail, I want my mesh triangles to be inside the blue boundary but at the moment the mesh seems to be created outside the blue boundary (Plot_2).I attached the R code, the data, plot_1 and plot _2 in the zip file.Would you have any advice to solve this problem?

Thank you in advance
Morgane

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] INLA coast Boundary mesh problem
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] INLA coast Boundary mesh problem
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the INLA/fmesher code, as well as the "sf" standard, defines the
interior of a polygon by what direction the boundary is traversed,
specifically counterclockwise for the boundary of a polygon when seen
from "above".
Unfortunately, lots of code either has a different convention, or
fails to properly convert between the two different conventions (e.g.
the geos library has a clockwise convention, but the "sf" package
ignores that, so whenever sf calls
a libgeos method with a properly counterclockwise oriented polygon,
libgeos converts it to its clockwise convention, and sf doesn't
convert it back again afterwards).
There are different ways of "fixing" such polygons (but in general it
is impossible to "fix" as both orientations potentially carry
information that is lost when assuming the polygon should have a
certain orientation).
One is to reverse the coordinate order, and another is to ask sf to
guess the correct orientation, which is probably the easiest approach:

data$geometry <- sf::st_sfc(data$geometry, check_ring_dir = TRUE)

But apart from that, you might need to consider having an extension
outside the blue boundary as well; the edge in the ocean isn't a "hard
boundary", so having the model extend a bit would remove the spde
model boundary effects from the domain of interest.  You can have
larger triangles in that outer extension, so the computational cost is
only increased slightly.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] INLA coast Boundary mesh problem
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] INLA coast Boundary mesh problem
messages.body_plain:
See example code at
https://inlabru-org.github.io/fmesher/articles/basic_use.html
The principle is this:
fm_mesh_2d(..., boundary = list(first_boundary, outer_boundary),
max.edge = c(inner_max_edge, outer_max_edge))

Note that extending the mesh inland is also ok, for the same reason,
unless you need the structure to "block" the path between different
parts of the ocean. But in that case, you could apply a barrier spde
model to the mesh instead of the default spde models.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
That looks exactly what I am looking for. Thank you very much.

Is there a way of using that family in inlabru with my own design matrices and penalty matrices, i.e. allowing to model the precision in a model like this:

df <- list(y = y, X_1 = X_1, X_2 = X_2, K_1 = K_1, K_2 = K_2)

result <- bru(
      components =
        ~ Intercept(1) +
        lc1(seq_len(nrow(K_1)), model="generic0", Cmatrix=K_1, hyper = hyper_prior) +
        lc2(seq_len(nrow(K_2)), model="generic0", Cmatrix=K_2, hyper = hyper_prior),
      like(
        family = "gaussian",
        data = df,
        formula = y ~ Intercept + X_1 %*% lc1 + X_2 %*% lc2,
      ),
      options = list(
        control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor=TRUE)
      )
    )

messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

So, what I am trying to do is to predict how my seabird distribution is going to change at sea.
I don't want any prediction on land because my covariates are oceanic variables.
Do you think in that case I should use a barrier spde model?

Thank you
Morgane

On Friday, 1 December 2023 at 13:55:46 UTC Finn Lindgren wrote:
> See example code at
> https://inlabru-org.github.io/fmesher/articles/basic_use.html
> The principle is this:
> fm_mesh_2d(..., boundary = list(first_boundary, outer_boundary),
> max.edge = c(inner_max_edge, outer_max_edge))
>
> Note that extending the mesh inland is also ok, for the same reason,
> unless you need the structure to "block" the path between different
> parts of the ocean. But in that case, you could apply a barrier spde
> model to the mesh instead of the default spde models.
>
> Finn
>
> On Fri, 1 Dec 2023 at 13:43, Morgane Declerck
> <morgane....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Finn,
> >
> > Thank you very much for your answer.
> > Yes, I think you are right I need to consider having an extension toward the edge of the ocean, but I am not sure how to do that.
> > Would you recommend to do that?
> >
> > Thank you very much
> >
> > Morgane
> >
> > On Friday, 1 December 2023 at 13:35:47 UTC Finn Lindgren wrote:
> >>
> >> Hi,
> >>
> >> the INLA/fmesher code, as well as the "sf" standard, defines the
> >> interior of a polygon by what direction the boundary is traversed,
> >> specifically counterclockwise for the boundary of a polygon when seen
> >> from "above".
> >> Unfortunately, lots of code either has a different convention, or
> >> fails to properly convert between the two different conventions (e.g.
> >> the geos library has a clockwise convention, but the "sf" package
> >> ignores that, so whenever sf calls
> >> a libgeos method with a properly counterclockwise oriented polygon,
> >> libgeos converts it to its clockwise convention, and sf doesn't
> >> convert it back again afterwards).
> >> There are different ways of "fixing" such polygons (but in general it
> >> is impossible to "fix" as both orientations potentially carry
> >> information that is lost when assuming the polygon should have a
> >> certain orientation).
> >> One is to reverse the coordinate order, and another is to ask sf to
> >> guess the correct orientation, which is probably the easiest approach:
> >>
> >> data$geometry <- sf::st_sfc(data$geometry, check_ring_dir = TRUE)
> >>
> >> But apart from that, you might need to consider having an extension
> >> outside the blue boundary as well; the edge in the ocean isn't a "hard
> >> boundary", so having the model extend a bit would remove the spde
> >> model boundary effects from the domain of interest. You can have
> >> larger triangles in that outer extension, so the computational cost is
> >> only increased slightly.
> >>
> >> Finn
> >>
> >> On Fri, 1 Dec 2023 at 13:15, Morgane Declerck
> >> <morgane....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >> >

I attached and plotted the data in the zip file. Plot_1, shows the red dots which are the locations of the points to create the mesh triangles inside the FOF_bound_sf. In Plot_2, I am creating the mesh using inla. mesh.create () function, but the mesh seems to be outside my FOF_bound_sf and not inside. In detail, I want my mesh triangles to be inside the blue boundary but at the moment the mesh seems to be created outside the blue boundary (Plot_2).I attached the R code, the data, plot_1 and plot _2 in the zip file.Would you have any advice to solve this problem?
> >> >

messages.body_plain:
this should be fixed now and will be available in the next build

On Thu, 2023-11-30 at 13:03 -0800, Scott Foster wrote:

> Hi,
>
> We've run into some issues with using a cloglog model for binary data
> (reproducibile in a simple glm).   In particular, we're getting a
> message of (e.g.) "GMRFLib_2order_approx: rescue NAN/INF values in
> logl for idx=789" for each observation (and seemingly for each/many
> iterations).  The problem is not produced when using a logit link or
> when using the glm() function from base R.
>
> The model does contain an offset, which has large values, but
> reducing/removing this doesn't seem to have any effect.
>
> I don't know how to fix this problem.  I reckon (uneducated guesses
> really) that
>
> 1) It is a user error
> 2) There is numerical overflow issues (so that predictions are very
> slightly above (below) 1 (0))
> 3) The starting values are very far from the max
> 4) some combination of 3 and 4.
>
> I have put code and simulated data in a dropbox folder.  Let me know
> if you can't access it.
> https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/00e4dko767yn42gnv1zoz/cloglogIssue1.R?rlkey=lr5gbo3488b7kyqt6z662yw2z&dl=0
> .  Script is pasted below (but data still on dropbox).
>
> Any help is appreciated. Thanks,
>
> Scott
>
>
> library( INLA)
>
> #data available from
> https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/tihsg9da53c6ar5z50vet/datPA.RDS?rlkey=im06zt0jnlssz1izpexsne346&dl=0
>
> datPA <- readRDS( "~/play/cloglogIssues/datPA.RDS")
>
> ############
> #Fit some models using glm()
> fmGLM <- list()
> #Fit the model that simulated the data. Note offset and pretty small
> intercept (negative on link scale)
> #The fit 'works', up to some possible quasi-separation issues (haven't
> investigated)
> fmGLM$cloglog <- glm( PA ~ 1+SoilMoisture+bio_4,
> offset=log(transectArea), data=datPA, family=binomial(link="cloglog"))
> #estimates are quite similar to those used to simulate (1.25 and -
> 0.85)
> summary( fmGLM$cloglog)
> fmGLM$logit <- glm( PA ~ 1+SoilMoisture+bio_4,
> offset=log(transectArea), data=datPA, family=binomial(link="logit"))
> #estimates are more dissimilar, but that is probably because there is
> a different link.
> summary( fmGLM$logit)
>
> ###########
> #Now let's try the same with inla()
> fmINLA <- list()
> fmINLA$cloglog <- inla(PA ~ 1+SoilMoisture+bio_4, offset = log(
> datPA$transectArea), data=datPA, Ntrials=1,
>                  family = "binomial",
> control.family=list(link="cloglog"), inla.mode="classic")
> #this seems to have more-or-less failed with lots of errors like:
> #...
> #GMRFLib_2order_approx: rescue NAN/INF values in logl for idx=990
> #GMRFLib_2order_approx: rescue NAN/INF values in logl for idx=991
> #GMRFLib_2order_approx: rescue NAN/INF values in logl for idx=992
> #GMRFLib_2order_approx: rescue NAN/INF values in logl for idx=993
> #...
> #In fact, there appears to be an error for each datum, possibly for
> each iteration of the optimisation
> #Perhaps not surprisingly, the estimates are... not similar.  Probably
> stuck at starting values?
> summary( fmINLA$cloglog)
>
> #will logit be any different?
> fmINLA$logit <- inla(PA ~ 1+SoilMoisture+bio_4, offset = log(
> datPA$transectArea), data=datPA, Ntrials=1,
>                        family = "binomial",
> control.family=list(link="logit"), inla.mode="classic")
> #no warning/error messages
> #and the estimates appear to be very similar to those from the logit
> GLM.
> summary( fmINLA$logit)
>
> #########
> #FWIW, add strong priors to effects may 'help' with the possible
> quasi-separation.
> fmINLA$cloglog_prior1 <- inla(PA ~ 1+SoilMoisture+bio_4, offset = log(
> datPA$transectArea), data=datPA, Ntrials=1,
>                  family = "binomial",
> control.family=list(link="cloglog"), inla.mode="classic",
> 		 control.fixed=list(mean=0, prec=1/0.1))
> #same errors and similar summary
>
> #what about when the intercept prior is shifted to be negative -- may
> affect starting values?
> fmINLA$cloglog_prior2 <- inla(PA ~ 1+SoilMoisture+bio_4, offset = log(
> datPA$transectArea), data=datPA, Ntrials=1,
>                  family = "binomial",
> control.family=list(link="cloglog"), inla.mode="classic",
> 		 control.fixed=list(mean.intercept=-15,
> prec.intercept=1))
>
> ##########
> #FWIW, reducing scale of offset or removing completely doesn't seem to
> solve the problem either
> #is it a problem with the size of the offset?
> #no, but there are fewer NAN/INF warnings
> fmINLA$smallerOffset <- inla(PA ~ 1+SoilMoisture+bio_4, offset = log(
> datPA$transectArea/1000000), data=datPA, Ntrials=1,
>                  family = "binomial",
> control.family=list(link="cloglog"), inla.mode="classic",
> 		 control.fixed=list(mean.intercept=-15,
> prec.intercept=1))
>
> fmINLA$noOffset <- inla(PA ~ 1+SoilMoisture+bio_4, offset = 0,
> data=datPA, Ntrials=1,
>                  family = "binomial",
> control.family=list(link="cloglog"), inla.mode="classic",
> 		 control.fixed=list(mean.intercept=-15,
> prec.intercept=1))
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Since the birds can fly over land, and there’s no reason to assume Neumann spde boundaries to be better at the coastline than a stationary model, you can simply ignore the estimation results over land. That they exist in the computational model doesn’t mean you need to interpret them in any way.

The barrier model would be needed e.g. if you were modelling fish in an archipelago, where they cannot swim across islands.

Finn

messages.subject: Tune spatial model run with heteroskedastic noise
messages.subject_clean: Tune spatial model run with heteroskedastic noise
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am aiming to do a model comparison who features an INLA run. This is a spatial model with heteroskadistic Gaussian noise. Is it possible to make the following script better ?
It is not possible to make the mesh any simpler for the sake of the comparison (the spatial locations are already mapping several observations and I would like to test several methods with the same dimension). But maybe the control.family could be better ?

Thank you in advance
Sébastien

#############
# load data #
#############

observed_field = readRDS("train_field.RDS")
coords = readRDS("train_locs.RDS")

#################
# get inla mesh #
#################

lonlat_CRS = sp::CRS("+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84 +no_defs +ellps=WGS84 +towgs84=0,0,0")
prmesh = INLA::inla.mesh.2d(coords)
prmesh$n
plot(prmesh)

##############
# Covariates #
##############

# train covariates
X = coords
X_split = split(X, col(X)); names(X_split) = c("coord_1", "coord_2")

# get PP at INLA mesh nodes #
PP = Bidart::get_PP(
  observed_locs = prmesh$loc, # spatial sites
  matern_range = .2,
  n_PP = 50, # number of knots
  m = 15 # number of NNGP parents
)

PP_basis_prmesh = as.matrix(Matrix::solve(PP$sparse_chol, diag(1, nrow(PP$sparse_chol), PP$n_PP))[-seq(PP$n_PP),][PP$idx,])
Bidart::plot_pointillist_painting(prmesh$loc, PP_basis_prmesh[,1])
PP_basis_obs = PP_basis_prmesh[match(split(coords, row(coords)), split(prmesh$loc[,-3], row(prmesh$loc[,-3]))),]

#######################################
# nonstationary heteroscedastic noise #
#######################################

X_noise_split = split(PP_basis_obs, col(PP_basis_obs)); names(X_noise_split) = paste("PP_", seq(ncol(PP_basis_obs)), sep="")

# PP_basis_obs corresponds to observations of the covariates
# ***at the coordinates of the observations***
A_noise = Matrix::Diagonal(n=nrow(PP_basis_obs), x=1)
# A noise is an identity matrix with
# as many rows and columns as the number of observations
spde_noise <- INLA::inla.spde2.generic(
  M0 = Matrix::Diagonal(n=nrow(PP_basis_obs), x=1.0),
  M1 = Matrix::Diagonal(n=nrow(PP_basis_obs), x=0.0),
  M2 = Matrix::Diagonal(n=nrow(PP_basis_obs), x=0.0),
  B0 = cbind(0, PP_basis_obs), B1 = matrix(0, 1, 1+ ncol(PP_basis_obs)),
  B2 = matrix(0, 1, 1+ ncol(PP_basis_obs)),
  theta.mu <http://theta.mu> = rep(0,ncol(PP_basis_obs)),
  theta.Q = diag(rep(.00001,ncol(PP_basis_obs))), # very weak prior
  transform = "identity")

########################################
# stationary spatially coherent effect #
########################################
 A_field = INLA::inla.spde.make.A(prmesh, # SPDE mesh
                                  loc=coords # coordinates of the observations of the interest variable
                                  )
 spde_spatially_coherent = INLA::inla.spde2.matern(mesh = prmesh, alpha=2)

#################################################
# combining noise and spatially coherent effect #
#################################################

stk <- INLA::inla.stack(
  data = list(y = observed_field),
  A = list(A_noise,
           A_field,
           1
           ),
  effects=list(
    INLA::inla.spde.make.index(
      name = "heteroscedastic.noise",
      spde_noise$n.spde), #the noise index
    # the length of the noise index is equal to the number of observations
    INLA::inla.spde.make.index(
      name = "spatial.field",
      spde_spatially_coherent$n.spde),  #the spatial field index
    # the length of the spatial index is equal to the number of mesh nodes
    X_split #the covariates
  ))

formula = observed_field ~
  - 1 + # removing superfluous intercept
  coord_1 + coord_2 +  # fixed effects
  f(heteroscedastic.noise, model = spde_noise)+ # heteroskedastic Gaussian noise
  f(spatial.field, model = spde_spatially_coherent) # spatially coherent random effect

#################################
# run  with nonstationary noise #
#################################

clik <- list(hyper = list(prec = list(initial = 20,
                                      fixed = TRUE)))
res <- INLA::inla(formula, data = INLA::inla.stack.data(stk), control.family = clik,
             control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, A = INLA::inla.stack.A(stk)), verbose = T)

saveRDS(res, "runINLA.RDS")

messages.subject_clean: Spatio-temporal INLA: no consecutive years of sample presence
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am builiding a spatio-temporal inla zero-inflated Poisson model for 5 different plant species, that were sampled on the coast for 6 years. For two species, their presence was not notified for one or more years during sampling.

For example, plant X was notified in 2017 - 2018 - 2019 - 2022, but in 2020 and 2021 it was missing. This gives me problems in forming my INLA stack, as my projector matrix and spatial weights can not be "aligned" (2022 has the value of 6, but 4 and 5 are missing). Is there a way to overcome this issue?
Adding years with no data on the species to the entire dataset could perhaps be a solution?

Kind regards,
Charlotte

If it was reported missing in 2020/21, that would also be an observation and should be accounted for. If there was no effort in 2020/21 then that’s a different situation, and whether you need to do anything special depends on your model setup. Normally, one would just associate whatever observations one has with the model; the doesn’t need to be any consistent pattern between different years.
Finn

messages.subject: Spatiotemporal INLA: problems with fitting model in R-INLA.
messages.subject_clean: Spatiotemporal INLA: problems with fitting model in R-INLA.
messages.body_plain:
Hello everybody,

I am building a spatiotemporal hurdle model for suicide mortality data using R-INLA.
I am analyzing monthly suicide data for 250 municipalities in Korea from 2010 to 2021. Data contains many zeros, and that's why the Hurdle model.

Whenever I run the inla(..) code using verbose=T, it seems that R-INLA computation works for some time then it stops at a point, giving no results.
Here is the code that I used:

su<-read.csv("~/TOTAL_monthly_suicide_regression_long.csv")
#Standardization of the variables
su[,c(8:15)] <- sapply(su[,c(8:15)],scale)

# Install INLA from source
install.packages("INLA",repos=c(getOption("repos"),INLA="https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/testing
"), type="binary", dep=TRUE)

library(INLA)
library(spdep)
map<-rgdal::readOGR("SIG_2019.shp", encoding = 'utf-8')
nb <- poly2nb(map)
nb2INLA("map.adj", nb)
g <- inla.read.graph(filename = "map.adj")
#Splitting data like hurdle model
#Index of group 1
idx1<- as.integer(su$Suicide_counts) ==0
table(idx1)
#Empty response
yy <- matrix (NA,ncol=2, nrow=nrow(su))

#Add data

yy[idx1,1]<- as.integer(su$Suicide_counts)[idx1]
yy[!idx1,2]<- as.integer(su$Suicide_counts)[!idx1]
summary(yy)
#Create two different intercepts
II <- yy
II[II>0] <-1

S<- length(unique(su$SIG_CD))
Temp <- length(unique(su$Idtime))

names(su)
data1 <- data.frame(count= as.integer(su$Suicide_counts),
                    pop=as.integer(su$Population),
                    idx=rep(1:S, Temp),
                     idx.int <http://idx.int>= rep(1:S, Temp),
                    temp= rep(1:Temp, each=S),
                    temp1= rep(1:Temp, each=S),
                    temp.int <http://temp.int>= rep(1:Temp, each=S),
                    intercept=II,
                    stress_percp =su$stress_percp,
                    fin_indp = su$fin_indp,
                     green_space =su$green_space,
                   Healthprom =  su$Healthprom,
                   smoking = su$smoking,
                   singleh = su$singleh,
                   Population = su$Population)
#fitting

#install.packages("MatrixModels", type = "source")

formula <- yy ~  intercept.1 + intercept.2 +
  f(idx, model = "bym", graph = g, constr= TRUE) +
  f(temp, model = "rw1") +
  f(temp1, model = "iid") +
  f(idx.int <http://idx.int>, model = "besag", graph = g, group = temp.int <http://temp.int>, control.group = list(model = "rw1")) +
  stress_percp + fin_indp + green_space + Healthprom + smoking + singleh

# Fit the model
suicide_res <- inla(
  formula,
  offset = log(pop),
  data = data1,
  family = c("binomial", "nbinomial"),
  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE, waic = TRUE)
)

The code doesn't give results while fitting the model. I am a beginner in R-INLA, so any suggestions would be highly appreciated.

Regards,
Trishna

messages.body_plain:
two points:

- apart from different intercepts, the linear predictor for the
probability of zero is the same as for the probability of being
greater than zero as you declared all the other terms in the formula
to be the same for both parts. Why modeling the positives with the
'nbinomial' likelihood, which includes zero and is not truncated. Have
you compared with the "zeroinflatednbinomial0" likelihood?

- the model component specified with

  f(idx.int <http://idx.int>, model = "besag", graph = g, group = temp.int <http://temp.int>,
control.group = list(model = "rw1"))

specifies a model of size n*k, where n is the number of areas and k is
the number of times. However, this model specification misses
accounting for n-1 of the n+k-1 constraints needed. I suggest defining
the structure matrix and use model = 'generic0' along with the
constraints (or the inla.knmodels() function).

Elias

Hi,

I tried to find what the following code does

# get PP at INLA mesh nodes #
PP = Bidart::get_PP(
  observed_locs = prmesh$loc, # spatial sites
  matern_range = .2,
  n_PP = 50, # number of knots
  m = 15 # number of NNGP parents
)

but I didn't find the Bidart package.

I guess some kind of basis functions were defined over the spatial
domain. Then the inla.spde2.generic() machinery was used to build the
heteroskedastic gaussian noise with n_PP (=50???) parameters.

I would start with lower n_PP and increase gradually until it stops
making sense.

The new gaussian likelihood may be an option in this case, see
inla.doc("GGaussian").

Best,
Leo Bastos

messages.subject: Version 23.12.06 && PARDISO
messages.subject_clean: Version 23.12.06 && PARDISO
messages.body_plain:
Version 23.12.06 (testing with R-4.3) now include the new PARDISO-
version-8 libraries, which you can get/buy a license from, at
www.panua.ch <http://www.panua.ch>  The license conditions are beyond our control.

However,

* Windows is not yet supported. the windows binary they provide does not
'work' for us, and a new build using a different compiler(s) has been
requested. if that happens, Windows builds will be updated.

* Fedora39 (and maybe other very 'new' distro's?). You might experience
half speed compared to older versions and recently it started (for me)
to produce internal (in PARIDSO) memory errors. running in serial mode I
think is fine, but that defy the purpose. This bug/regression was
reported some weeks ago.

* It seems to run fine on various Ubuntu installations.

As said before. We're working on an alternative open-source solution,
but this is a lot of work and it take time. We hope in first half of
2024.

H

--
Håvard Rue
he...@r-inla.org

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I’m trying to estimate a coregionalization model with the new version 23.12.06 of INLA and Pardiso, but after a while,  I have this error:

Segmentation fault
Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() :
  The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully.
  If this does not help, please contact the developers at <he...@r-inla.org>.
Calls: inla -> inla.core.safe
Execution halted
I don't think is a RAM or CPU problem  (the server has 40 CPU core and 377 GB RAM)
R version 4.3.2 (2023-10-31)
Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu (64-bit)
Running under: Debian GNU/Linux trixie/sid

#Coregionalization model ----

form <-
  y ~ 0 + Intercept.pm25 + Intercept.pm10 +  AOD550  + PM25 + PM10 +  windspeed10m +
  PBLH_HH00 + PBLH_HH12 + pres + tem2 + cumulprec + altitudedem_std + i_surface_std +  d_a1_std   +
  f(s1,
    model = spde,
    group = g1,
    control.group = ctr.g) +
  f(s2,
    model = spde,
    group = g2,
    control.group = ctr.g) +
  f(
    s12,
    copy = "s1",
    group = g12,
    fixed = FALSE,
    hyper = hyper
  )

spde <-
  inla.spde2.pcmatern(
    mesh = mesh,
    alpha = 2,
    constr = FALSE,
    prior.range = c(100, 0.8), # P(range < 100 km) = 0.8
    prior.sigma = c(0.8, 0.2) # P(sigma > 0.8) = 0.2
  )

 inla(form, rep('gaussian', 2),
       data=inla.stack.data(stack,spde=spde),
       control.family = list(hyper.eps, hyper.eps),
       verbose=TRUE,
       control.compute = list(cpo=F,waic=F,dic=T,config=TRUE),
       control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 1, prec=0.01,mean.intercept=0),
       control.predictor =list(A=inla.stack.A(stack),compute=T) )->inla.out

The log is attached

Thank you!
Maria Antonietta Reatini

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sébastien,

Inla can provide leave-one-out log-predictive-density scores directly (log(CPO)), but I think you’re asking about more general predictive scores, e.g. with hold-out data?

There’s a vignette discussing this in the inlabru context at https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/prediction_scores.html <https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/prediction_scores.html#poisson-model-example>
That discusses the general problem of computing posterior prediction scores as well as gives more details in the case of Poisson count predictions.
For plain inla, the same techniques can be used, by directly calling inla.posterior.sample() and postprocessing the output (thats what the inlabru generate() and predict() functions do).

Finn

messages.subject: distance sampling with random effects
messages.subject_clean: distance sampling with random effects
messages.body_plain:
hello all:

i am fitting distance functions to data using inlabru and the
following example:
https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/2d_lgcp_distancesampling.html

in the distance models there is a shape parameter. my distance data has
multiple species and i am wondering if i can make my shape parameter
a random effect that varies by species, or otherwise a fixed effect by species.
some species have very few observations (i.e., 1 observation), hence
shrinkage toward a mean would be nice.

any advice for how to do that? here is some reproducible code for a single
species model and then a dataset with 3 species if it is helpful to demonstrate,

Thank you!

# libraries
library(inlabru)
library(fmesher)
library(INLA)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)

# data
mexdolphin <- mexdolphin_sf # from example
mexdolphin2 <- mexdolphin$points %>% mutate(species_idx=1) %>% # add more species
  bind_rows(sample_frac(mexdolphin$points %>% st_drop_geometry(), size=.5) %>% mutate(species_idx=2)) %>%
  bind_rows(sample_frac(mexdolphin$points %>% st_drop_geometry(), size=.25) %>% mutate(species_idx=3))

# distance function
hn <- function(distance, sigma) {
  exp(-0.5 * (distance / sigma)^2)
}
sigma <- function(x) {
  bru_forward_transformation(qexp, x, rate = 1 / 8)
}

# model
formula <- distance ~ log(hn(distance, sigma(sigma_theta))) + Intercept
cmp <- ~ sigma_theta(1, prec.linear = 1) + Intercept(1)
dfit <- lgcp(
  components = cmp,
  mexdolphin$points,
  domain = list(distance = fm_mesh_1d(seq(0, 8, length.out = 30))),
  formula = formula,
  options = list(bru_initial = list(sigma_theta = 1, Intercept = 3))
)

# prediction
distdf <- data.frame(distance = seq(0, 8, length.out = 100))
detfun <- predict(dfit, distdf, ~ hn(distance, sigma(sigma_theta)))
plot(detfun)
summary(detfun) # this how to get average detecion probability?

# plot
hnline <- data.frame(distance = detfun$distance, p = detfun$mean,
                     lower = detfun$q0.025, upper = detfun$q0.975)
wts <- diff(hnline$distance)
wts[1] <- wts[1] / 2
wts <- c(wts, wts[1])
hnarea <- sum(wts * hnline$p)
n <- length(mexdolphin$points$distance)
scale <- n / hnarea
hnline$En <- hnline$p * scale
hnline$En.lower <- hnline$lower * scale
hnline$En.upper <- hnline$upper * scale
dlines <- rbind(
  cbind(hnline, model = "Half-normal")
)
ggplot(data.frame(mexdolphin$points)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = distance), breaks = seq(0, 8, length.out = 9),
                 alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = distance), y = 0.2, shape = "|", size = 3) +
  geom_line(data = dlines, aes(x = distance, y = En, group = model,
                               col = model))

# three species plot
ggplot(data.frame(mexdolphin2)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = distance), breaks = seq(0, 8, length.out = 9),
                 alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = distance), y = 0.2, shape = "|", size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~species_idx)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tim,

there are two issues to deal with here:
1. How to model the individual species densities.
2. How to construct a "sigma" parameter model that handles
low-prevalence species in a robust way.

For 1., the simplest option is when the same spatial pattern is
assumed for all species, with just a separate Intercept for each
species, but this part can be made much more complex...
In your example code, you're however not modelling the spatial
distribution at all, so you only need separate intercepts to account
for the different relative abundance;
  Intercept(species_idx, model = "iid", hyper=list(prec=list(...)))

For 2., one can view the model as a "marked point process, where the
mark influences the detectability". This type of model can be
constructed as a point process on the "product space", which
in your example would be "distance x species". Using the new
"marginal" feature, and without attempting to "borrow strength"
between species:

formula <- distance + species_idx ~ log(hn(distance, sigma)) + Intercept
cmp <- ~
       sigma(species_idx,
          model = "iid",
          hyper=list(prec=list(initial=0, fixed = TRUE)),

Intercept = rep(3, n_species))))

bru_mapper_marginal(qexp, rate = 1 / 8)) +

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Log- density score for Gaussian observations
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

First, thank Finn for everything ! I will look into it !

Haavard, as for your remark, in the Gaussian setting, I feel that the formula with the log inside the \int is some Bayesian extension of the Mean Squared Error, R-squared, and so on.
we get MSE = \sum((y-X\hat\beta - \hat w)^2)
\hat w being the chosen point estimate of the latent field, \hat\beta the point estimate of the regression coefficients for the fixed effects.
If we want to predict a (Gaussian) distribution instead of fixed values, we can do this by weighting by the noise standard deviation \hat s.
 MSE = \sum(( (y-X\hat\beta - \hat w) / \hat s)^2)
Here for example, if we have a heteroskedastic noise, instead of having a brutish MSE who is happy when the squares are low and angry when the squares are high, we get something that will assess the confidence with which the prediction is done, and punish both errors made confidently and good answers made hesitantly.
But then again, we have a Bayesian model so we have some incertitude on the parameters. My way to plug that in is to integrate over \beta, w, and s, giving the "log-inside" formula.
Do you think I am overlooking something there ?

Thanks to you all
Sébastien

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Log- density score for Gaussian observations
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I didn’t notice you didn’t have the version Haavard suggested, and instead used the expectation of the conditional score,

Eλ|data[S(Fλ,y)]

This issue is discussed in the vignette; in particular, it mentions the problems with improper scores this appears to result in, see https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/prediction_scores.html#posterior-expectation-of-conditional-scores
I would strongly encourage you to look up the Gneiting and Raftery JASA paper (mid-2000s) on proper scoring rules.

(Y-mu)^2/s^2 is not a proper score, as it can be reduced to zero by choosing s=infty.
But if you add log(s^2), it becomes a proper score(the Dawid-Sebastiani score, which is the same as the log-score for Gaussian data).

Finn

This is discussed in the vignette. The main part of the vignette is about how to compute scores based on the full posterior predictive distribution. This is well-defined, so should be a “safe” choice.  The version of taking the posterior expectation of scores for conditional posterior predictions (which is what you proposed doing) is however potentially problematic. This is what is mentioned in the section towards the end of the vignette.

> This is discussed in the vignette. The main part of the vignette is about how to compute scores based on the full posterior predictive distribution. This is well-defined, so should be a “safe” choice.  The version of taking the posterior expectation of scores for conditional posterior predictions (which is what you proposed doing) is however potentially problematic. This is what is mentioned in the section towards the end of the vignette.
> Finn
>
> > On 14 Dec 2023, at 14:42, Sébastien Coube <sebasti...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > ﻿I am afraid that I understood what you mean !

> > Le jeudi 14 décembre 2023 à 14:27:45 UTC+1, Finn Lindgren a écrit :
> > > Ok, I see!
> > > But there are still possible issues with using the expectation of conditional prediction scores instead of the scores for the full posterior predictions, so consider that carefully.

> > > > > I would strongly encourage you to look up the Gneiting and Raftery JASA paper (mid-2000s) on proper scoring rules.
> > > > >

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] distance sampling with random effects
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] distance sampling with random effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn, All,

Finn, I tried the code you sent and got the first model with random intercepts to work after installing the latest inlabru version. The second model with the sigma_log_factor component, I'm not so sure. The model computes but when I try to predict and plot, I get funky plots. That could be because I specified model options wrong or that I am giving predict() the wrong formula. If you you wouldn't mind looking over the latest script, below, I'd appreciate it. Once it is for-sure working I will add the final script here for others. Or I am happy to work it into the original vignette if you think it would be helpful. Doing a multispecies distance function like this is a common objective for ecologists.

Thanks!
Tim

# libraries
library(inlabru) # >= v 2.10 !!!

library(fmesher)
library(INLA)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)

# data
mexdolphin <- mexdolphin_sf # from example
mexdolphin2 <- mexdolphin$points %>% mutate(species_idx=1) %>% # add more species
  bind_rows(sample_frac(mexdolphin$points %>% st_drop_geometry(), size=.5) %>% mutate(species_idx=2)) %>%
  bind_rows(sample_frac(mexdolphin$points %>% st_drop_geometry(), size=.25) %>% mutate(species_idx=3))

# distance function
hn <- function(distance, sigma) {
  exp(-0.5 * (distance / sigma)^2)
}
sigma <- function(x) {
  bru_forward_transformation(qexp, x, rate = 1 / 8)
}

# 1 species model 1

formula <- distance ~ log(hn(distance, sigma(sigma_theta))) + Intercept
cmp <- ~ sigma_theta(1, prec.linear = 1) + Intercept(1)
dfit <- lgcp(
  components = cmp,
  mexdolphin$points,
  domain = list(distance = fm_mesh_1d(seq(0, 8, length.out = 30))),
  formula = formula,
  options = list(bru_initial = list(sigma_theta = 1, Intercept = 3))
)

# prediction model 1

distdf <- data.frame(distance = seq(0, 8, length.out = 100))
detfun <- predict(dfit, distdf, ~ hn(distance, sigma(sigma_theta)))
plot(detfun)
summary(detfun)

# 1 species plot

hnline <- data.frame(distance = detfun$distance, p = detfun$mean,
                     lower = detfun$q0.025, upper = detfun$q0.975)
wts <- diff(hnline$distance)
wts[1] <- wts[1] / 2
wts <- c(wts, wts[1])
hnarea <- sum(wts * hnline$p)
n <- length(mexdolphin$points$distance)
scale <- n / hnarea
hnline$En <- hnline$p * scale
hnline$En.lower <- hnline$lower * scale
hnline$En.upper <- hnline$upper * scale
dlines <- rbind(
  cbind(hnline, model = "Half-normal")
)
ggplot(data.frame(mexdolphin$points)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = distance), breaks = seq(0, 8, length.out = 9),
                 alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = distance), y = 0.2, shape = "|", size = 3) +
  geom_line(data = dlines, aes(x = distance, y = En, group = model,
                               col = model))

# initial three species plot

ggplot(data.frame(mexdolphin2)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = distance), breaks = seq(0, 8, length.out = 9),
                 alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = distance), y = 0.2, shape = "|", size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~species_idx)

# 3 species model 1
n_species <- length(unique(mexdolphin2$species_idx))
formula1 <- distance + species_idx ~ log(hn(distance, sigma)) + Intercept
cmp1 <- ~

  sigma(species_idx,
        model = "iid",
        hyper=list(prec=list(initial=0, fixed = TRUE)),
        marginal = bru_mapper_marginal(qexp, rate = 1 / 8)) +
  Intercept(species_idx, model = "iid",
            hyper=list(prec=list(initial = -2, fixed = TRUE)))

dfit1 <- lgcp(
  components = cmp1,
  mexdolphin2,

  domain = list(
    distance = fm_mesh_1d(seq(0, 8, length.out = 30)),

    species_idx = sort(unique(mexdolphin2$species_idx))),
  formula = formula1,

  options = list(bru_initial = list(sigma = rep(1, n_species),
                                    Intercept = rep(3, n_species))))

# 3 spp model 1 preds
distdf <- expand.grid(distance = seq(0, 8, length.out = 100),
                      species_idx=1:3)
detfun <- predict(dfit1, distdf, ~ hn(distance, sigma))
plot(detfun) + facet_wrap(~species_idx)
detfun %>% group_by(species_idx) %>%
  summarise(mean_p_per_species=mean(mean))

# 3 species model 2
formula2 <- distance + species_idx ~ log(hn(distance,
                              sigma_common*exp(sigma_log_factor))) + Intercept
cmp2 <- ~

  sigma_common(1, prec.linear = 1, marginal =
                 bru_mapper_marginal(qexp, rate = 1 / 8)) +
  sigma_log_factor(species_idx,
                   model = "iid",
                   hyper=list(prec=list(initial=0, fixed = FALSE)),

                   constr = TRUE) +

  Intercept(species_idx, model = "iid",
            hyper=list(prec=list(initial = -2, fixed = TRUE)))

dfit2 <- lgcp(
  components = cmp2,
  mexdolphin2,

  domain = list(
    distance = fm_mesh_1d(seq(0, 8, length.out = 30)),

    species_idx = sort(unique(mexdolphin2$species_idx))),
  formula = formula2,
  options = list(bru_initial = list(sigma_common = 1,
                                    sigma_log_factor = rep(1, n_species),
                                    Intercept = rep(3, n_species))))

# 3 spp model 2 preds
distdf <- expand.grid(distance = seq(0, 8, length.out = 100),
                      species_idx=1:3)
detfun <- predict(dfit2, distdf, ~log(hn(distance,
                                       sigma_common*exp(sigma_log_factor))))
plot(detfun) + facet_wrap(~species_idx)
detfun %>% group_by(species_idx) %>%
  summarise(mean_p_per_species=mean(mean))

messages.body_plain:
A few bugs in your code... Corrected version of the second model below.
In short
- The initial values for sigma_log_factor need to respect the
sum-to-zero constraint. Starting them at zero works fine.
- You were predicting log(hn()) at the end, instead of hn().
I think that's all I needed to change; the results I get are now
similar for dfit1 and dfit2, with slightly narrower uncertainty bands
for dfit2, indicating that it did indeed "borrow strength" between the
species.
You should also set the parameters of the sigma_log_factor hyper
specification instead of relying on the defaults; who knows what they
mean in this context...

The bru_convergence_plot() figure indicates some wobbliness in the
convergence of the parameters for the least abundant species; not sure
if/how to improve that except by tightening the convergence detection
tolerance a bit; it is stable and has decreasing step lengths, but
oscillates around what would likely be the true optimum. The
oscillation is well within the posterior uncertainty bands though.

Finn

formula2 <- distance + species_idx ~ log(hn(distance,

sigma_common*exp(sigma_log_factor))) + Intercept
cmp2 <- ~
  sigma_common(1, prec.linear = 1, marginal =
                 bru_mapper_marginal(qexp, rate = 1 / 8)) +
  sigma_log_factor(species_idx,
                   model = "iid",
                   hyper=list(prec=list(initial=0,
                                        fixed = FALSE)),
                   constr = TRUE) +
  Intercept(species_idx, model = "iid",
            hyper=list(prec=list(initial = -2, fixed = TRUE)))
dfit2 <- lgcp(
  components = cmp2,
  mexdolphin2,
  domain = list(
    distance = fm_mesh_1d(seq(0, 8, length.out = 30)),
    species_idx = sort(unique(mexdolphin2$species_idx))),
  formula = formula2,
  options = list(bru_initial = list(sigma_common = 1,

                                    sigma_log_factor = rep(0, n_species),

                                    Intercept = rep(3, n_species))))

# 3 spp model 2 preds
distdf <- expand.grid(distance = seq(0, 8, length.out = 100),
                      species_idx=1:3)

detfun <- predict(dfit2, distdf, ~hn(distance,
                                         sigma_common*exp(sigma_log_factor)))

plot(detfun) + facet_wrap(~species_idx)
detfun %>% group_by(species_idx) %>%
  summarise(mean_p_per_species=mean(mean))

messages.body_plain:
Excellent! I'll send along a vignette in a month or so. In the meantime here is some rough code that works in case it is useful to others.

# libraries
library(inlabru) # >= v 2.10 !!!
library(fmesher)
library(INLA)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)

# data
mexdolphin <- mexdolphin_sf # from example
mexdolphin2 <- mexdolphin$points %>% mutate(species_idx=1) %>% # add more species
  bind_rows(sample_frac(mexdolphin$points %>% st_drop_geometry(), size=.5) %>% mutate(species_idx=2)) %>%
  bind_rows(sample_frac(mexdolphin$points %>% st_drop_geometry(), size=.25) %>% mutate(species_idx=3))

# distance function
hn <- function(distance, sigma) {
  exp(-0.5 * (distance / sigma)^2)
}
sigma <- function(x) {
  bru_forward_transformation(qexp, x, rate = 1 / 8)
}

# 1 species model 1
formula <- distance ~ log(hn(distance, sigma(sigma_theta))) + Intercept
cmp <- ~ sigma_theta(1, prec.linear = 1) + Intercept(1)
dfit <- lgcp(
  components = cmp,
  mexdolphin$points,
  domain = list(distance = fm_mesh_1d(seq(0, 8, length.out = 30))),
  formula = formula,
  options = list(bru_initial = list(sigma_theta = 1, Intercept = 3))
)

# prediction model 1
distdf <- data.frame(distance = seq(0, 8, length.out = 100))
detfun <- predict(dfit, distdf, ~ hn(distance, sigma(sigma_theta)))
plot(detfun)
summary(detfun)

# 1 species plot
hnline <- data.frame(distance = detfun$distance, p = detfun$mean,
                     lower = detfun$q0.025, upper = detfun$q0.975)
wts <- diff(hnline$distance)
wts[1] <- wts[1] / 2
wts <- c(wts, wts[1])
hnarea <- sum(wts * hnline$p)
n <- length(mexdolphin$points$distance)
scale <- n / hnarea
hnline$En <- hnline$p * scale
hnline$En.lower <- hnline$lower * scale
hnline$En.upper <- hnline$upper * scale
dlines <- rbind(
  cbind(hnline, model = "Half-normal")
)
ggplot(data.frame(mexdolphin$points)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = distance), breaks = seq(0, 8, length.out = 9),
                 alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = distance), y = 0.2, shape = "|", size = 3) +
  geom_line(data = dlines, aes(x = distance, y = En, group = model,
                               col = model))

# initial three species plot
ggplot(data.frame(mexdolphin2)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = distance), breaks = seq(0, 8, length.out = 9),
                 alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = distance), y = 0.2, shape = "|", size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~species_idx)

# 3 species model 1 --- random species intercepts

n_species <- length(unique(mexdolphin2$species_idx))
formula1 <- distance + species_idx ~ log(hn(distance, sigma)) + Intercept
cmp1 <- ~
  sigma(species_idx,
        model = "iid",
        hyper=list(prec=list(initial=0, fixed = TRUE)),
        marginal = bru_mapper_marginal(qexp, rate = 1 / 8)) +
  Intercept(species_idx, model = "iid",
            hyper=list(prec=list(initial = -2, fixed = TRUE)))
dfit1 <- lgcp(
  components = cmp1,
  mexdolphin2,
  domain = list(
    distance = fm_mesh_1d(seq(0, 8, length.out = 30)),
    species_idx = sort(unique(mexdolphin2$species_idx))),
  formula = formula1,
  options = list(bru_initial = list(sigma = rep(1, n_species),
                                    Intercept = rep(3, n_species))))

# 3 spp model 1 preds
distdf <- expand.grid(distance = seq(0, 8, length.out = 100),
                      species_idx=1:3)
detfun <- predict(dfit1, distdf, ~ hn(distance, sigma))
plot(detfun) + facet_wrap(~species_idx)
detfun %>% group_by(species_idx) %>%
  summarise(mean_p_per_species=mean(mean))

# 3 spp model 1 plot

hnline <- data.frame(distance = detfun$distance, p = detfun$mean,

                     lower = detfun$q0.025, upper = detfun$q0.975,
                     species_idx=detfun$species_idx)
scale_for_plots <- function(obs_dat=mexdolphin2, pred_dat=hnline){
  wts <- diff(pred_dat[,"distance"])

  wts[1] <- wts[1] / 2
  wts <- c(wts, wts[1])

  hnarea <- sum(wts * pred_dat[, "p"])
  n <- length(obs_dat$distance)

  scale <- n / hnarea

  pred_dat$En <- pred_dat[, "p"] * scale
  pred_dat$En.lower <- pred_dat[, "lower"] * scale
  pred_dat$En.upper <- pred_dat[, "upper"] * scale
  return(pred_dat)
}
out_df <- c()
for(i in 1:n_species){
  out_i <- scale_for_plots(obs_dat=mexdolphin2[mexdolphin2$species_idx==i, ],
                           pred_dat=hnline[hnline$species_idx==i, ])
  out_df <- rbind(out_df, out_i)
}
plot_dat <- out_df

ggplot(data.frame(mexdolphin2)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = distance),
                 breaks = seq(0, 8, length.out = 9),
                 alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = distance), y = 0.2, shape = "|", size = 3) +

  geom_ribbon(data = plot_dat,
              aes(x = distance, ymin = En.lower, ymax=En.upper, fill=factor(species_idx)),
              alpha=0.3) +
  geom_line(data = plot_dat, aes(x = distance, y = En)) +
  facet_wrap(~species_idx)

# 3 species model 2 --- random intercepts and shape parameters

formula2 <- distance + species_idx ~ log(hn(distance,
                              sigma_common*exp(sigma_log_factor))) + Intercept
cmp2 <- ~
  sigma_common(1, prec.linear = 1, marginal =
                 bru_mapper_marginal(qexp, rate = 1 / 8)) +
  sigma_log_factor(species_idx,
                   model = "iid",
                   hyper=list(prec=list(initial=0,
                                        fixed = FALSE)),
                   constr = TRUE) +
  Intercept(species_idx, model = "iid",
            hyper=list(prec=list(initial = -2, fixed = TRUE)))
dfit2 <- lgcp(
  components = cmp2,
  mexdolphin2,
  domain = list(
    distance = fm_mesh_1d(seq(0, 8, length.out = 30)),
    species_idx = sort(unique(mexdolphin2$species_idx))),
  formula = formula2,
  options = list(bru_initial = list(sigma_common = 1,
                                    sigma_log_factor = rep(0, n_species),
                                    Intercept = rep(3, n_species))))

# 3 spp model 2 preds
distdf <- expand.grid(distance = seq(0, 8, length.out = 100),
                      species_idx=1:3)
detfun <- predict(dfit2, distdf, ~hn(distance,
                                     sigma_common*exp(sigma_log_factor)))
plot(detfun) + facet_wrap(~species_idx)
detfun %>% group_by(species_idx) %>%
  summarise(mean_p_per_species=mean(mean))

# 3 spp model 2 plot

hnline <- data.frame(distance = detfun$distance, p = detfun$mean,

                     lower = detfun$q0.025, upper = detfun$q0.975,
                     species_idx=detfun$species_idx)
scale_for_plots <- function(obs_dat=mexdolphin2, pred_dat=hnline){
  wts <- diff(pred_dat[,"distance"])

  wts[1] <- wts[1] / 2
  wts <- c(wts, wts[1])

  hnarea <- sum(wts * pred_dat[, "p"])
  n <- length(obs_dat$distance)

  scale <- n / hnarea

  pred_dat$En <- pred_dat[, "p"] * scale
  pred_dat$En.lower <- pred_dat[, "lower"] * scale
  pred_dat$En.upper <- pred_dat[, "upper"] * scale
  return(pred_dat)
}

  out_df <- rbind(out_df, out_i)
}

messages.subject: Can INLA fit this gaussian random effects with the composite covariance matrix using rgeneric?
messages.subject_clean: Can INLA fit this gaussian random effects with the composite covariance matrix using rgeneric?
messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA group,

I have a spatio-temporal model, whose covariance matrix of the gaussian random effects write

 \left [ I_T\bigotimes B_{N}^{-1} \right ]\Omega_\epsilon \left [ I_T\bigotimes (B_{N}^{T})^{-1} \right ]

where
 B_{N} = I_N-\rho W_N.

\Omega_\epsilon = [{\sigma_e}^2 I_T+{\sigma_\mu}^2 J_T] \bigotimes I_N

 J_T is a T\times T matrix of ones, I_T is a  T\times T identity matrix and I_N is a  N\times N identity matrix.

Since \Omega_\epsilon has an additive form, is it possible to use rgeneric function to fit this model?

Thank you.
Charles

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Can INLA fit this gaussian random effects with the composite covariance matrix using rgeneric?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Can INLA fit this gaussian random effects with the composite covariance matrix using rgeneric?
messages.body_plain:
That look like a special CAR model with diagonal noise driver. If the W matrix is known and fixed and since Omega_epsilon is diagonal (hand hence has diagonal inverse) then yes, rgeneric and cgeneric should be doable. You’d need to write the precision version of the matrix instead of the covariance, but that looks trivial in this case.
Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] INLA report this error, how to fix it?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] INLA report this error, how to fix it?
messages.body_plain:
Warning: This is little technical.

At the mode of the hyperparameters, we estimate the Hessian matrix, and
its inverse its the estimated covariance matrix. Doing a linear
transformation into iid normals (using the eigen(cov)...), then this
warning says that when we look around in each of these new directions,
then it seems like the marginal variance is not what Hessian predict.
this is detected while correcting for skewness.

So in a way, we have two sources of information that is contradicting
each other, about the marginal variance for one (or more) linear
combinations of the hyperparameters. In recent INLA versions the default
behaviour is to believe the Hessian and override the local variance
information, with this option in 'control.inla'

hessian.correct.skewness.only: If TRUE (default) correct only skewness
          in the Hessian, for the hyperparameters. If FALSE, correct
          also variance. (This option is for experimental-mode only)

for some earlier versions (when we started to look into this), this
option was set to default FALSE, and earlier again, this problem was no
detected (which was eqv to FALSE).

Our newer experience with simulations, is that TRUE is the natural
default option.

when does this happens?  Usually when the log posterior is flat wrt one
of more of the hyperparameters, so its hard to get the variance right. A
more informative prior, or less flexible model, usually will make this
go away.

You can make a component that contains both parts of the model, for example like inla implements the bym models. Either as two independent blocks where you observe their sum, or as two dependent blocks where the \mu block is a hidden internal block, and \mu+u is the combined block that is observed in the predictor. The joint precision matrix for that is sparse.
Finn

messages.subject: Intercept meaning in dummy factor model
messages.subject_clean: Intercept meaning in dummy factor model
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a model that I built over a year ago, and for a reason I can no longer remember I followed the advice of another post in this group (possibly to help with identifiability?) I split the factor fixed effects into dummy 0/1 variables for each factor level. I then also have an intercept (specified =1) in the model. In this situation I am not sure what the intercept represents, if someone might know?

Here are my current thoughts

1. does it represent when all dummy variables are 0?
2. is it still a universal constant that is added to each dummy coefficient?
3. lastly, would it be recommended to remove in a model with a dummy factor variable?

Many thanks,
Sylvan

messages.body_plain:
1. Yes
2. It's not added to the coefficients. It's added to the combined effect predictor.
3. If the dummy variables are from a factor variable, so that they are never all 0 at the same time, you need to ensure identifiability in some way. One option is to not include an intercept. Another is to remove one of the dummy variables and use that factor level as a reference level.
Those options are exactly what happens mathematically with linear factor variable effects.
Finn

One more question: If one wanted to add another nuisance variable, say effort, to the distance detection function, would you so it like the code below? The code runs but the fit for effort is perfect which makes me think there is something funky.

# 3 species model 2
formula2 <- distance + species_idx ~ log(hn(distance,

                              sigma_common*exp(sigma_log_factor))) + Intercept + effort

cmp2 <- ~
  sigma_common(1, prec.linear = 1, marginal =
                 bru_mapper_marginal(qexp, rate = 1 / 8)) +
  sigma_log_factor(species_idx,
                   model = "iid",
                   hyper=list(prec=list(initial=0,
                                        fixed = FALSE)),
                   constr = TRUE) +

  effort(Effort, model="rw2", scale.model=T) +

  Intercept(species_idx, model = "iid",
            hyper=list(prec=list(initial = -2, fixed = TRUE)))

dfit2 <- lgcp(
  components = cmp2,
  mexdolphin2,
  domain = list(
    distance = fm_mesh_1d(seq(0, 8, length.out = 30)),
    species_idx = sort(unique(mexdolphin2$species_idx))),
  formula = formula2,
  options = list(bru_initial = list(sigma_common = 1,
                                    sigma_log_factor = rep(0, n_species),
                                    Intercept = rep(3, n_species))))

messages.subject_clean: N-mixture model example crashes
messages.body_plain:
Hello Haavard,

Looks like the n-mixture model code is broken. Below is a reproducible example from our paper. I know that there have been a lot of advances in INLA since that likelihood was built. What do you think it would take to fix it? Sorry I don't know how to go under the hood to fix it myself.

Best,
Tim

# libraries
library(INLA)
library(unmarked)

# data
data(mallard)
mallard.umf <- unmarkedFramePCount(y = mallard.y, siteCovs = mallard.site,
                                   obsCovs = mallard.obs)
mallard.umf[1:6, ]
length <- mallard.site[ , "length"]
elev <- mallard.site[ , "elev"]
forest <- mallard.site[ , "forest"]
mean.ivel <- rowMeans(mallard.obs$ivel, na.rm = T)
mean.ivel[is.na <http://is.na>(mean.ivel)] <- mean(mean.ivel, na.rm = T)
mean.date <- rowMeans(mallard.obs$date, na.rm = T)
mean.date.sq <- mean.date^2
mallard.inla.df <- data.frame(y1 = mallard.y[ , "y.1"],
                              y2 = mallard.y[ , "y.2"],
                              y3 = mallard.y[ , "y.3"],
                              length, elev, forest, mean.ivel,
                              mean.date, mean.date.sq)
round(head(mallard.inla.df), 3)
counts.and.count.covs <- inla.mdata(mallard.y, 1, length, elev, forest)

# inla result, CRASHES
out.inla.2 <- inla(counts.and.count.covs ~ 1 + mean.ivel + mean.date + mean.date.sq,
                      data = list(counts.and.count.covs = counts.and.count.covs,
                                  mean.ivel = mallard.inla.df$mean.ivel,
                                  mean.date = mallard.inla.df$mean.date,
                                  mean.date.sq = mallard.inla.df$mean.date.sq),
                      family = "nmixnb")
summary(out.inla.2, digits = 3)

messages.body_plain:
The correct code for this in the case of spatial modelling depends on how the effort varies. If it’s a function of location, the component input needs to be given in such a way that inlabru can evaluate it for arbitrary locations; you cannot supply precomputed values, but should instead e.g. store it as a terra raster.

But since you don’t have space in your model it’s less clear what the intended model is meant to be. Every model component in the point process must be a function of the domain variables, I.e. here distance and species_idx. So effort would need to be a function of distance and species_idx _only_. How to code that depends on the storage…  what does the effort depend on? If it depends on location, you need to either make a spatial model, or potentially make “effort” a dimension of the point process?  I’ll need more details to give an accurate answer.
Finn

messages.subject: Setting a covariate prior in a proportional hazards model
messages.subject_clean: Setting a covariate prior in a proportional hazards model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am looking to set a prior on covariate in a proportional hazards model. Based on the following examples, I am not sure I understand how the prior influences the covariate effect estimate. I adapted some code from the Bayesian inference with INLA book (https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-survival.html#semi-parametric-estimation-cox-proportional-hazards) below.  With no fixed effect prior, the model reports mean = -0.047 and sd = 0.179 for trt. Changing the mean between 1, -1, 10, and -10 with a constant precision (of 10 for example) on the prior resulted in consistent estimates for trt. Increasing the precision would increase the estimate closer to 0, and decrease the standard deviation. Am I missing something here? Thanks so much.

veteran$time.m <- round(veteran$time / 30, 3)
sinla.vet <- inla.surv(veteran$time.m, veteran$status)

# No trt prior
coxinla.vet <- inla(sinla.vet ~  1 + trt, data = veteran,
                    family = "coxph",
                    control.hazard = list(hyper = list(prec = list(param = c(0.001, 0.001)))))
summary(coxinla.vet) # beta <- -0.047 (+/-0.179)

# Prior on trt - change mean and precision as needed
coxinla.vet2 <- inla(sinla.vet ~ 1   + trt, data = veteran,
                    family = "coxph",
                    control.hazard = list(hyper = list(prec = list(param = c(0.001, 0.001)))),
                    control.fixed = list(mean = list(trt = 1), prec = list(trt=10)))
summary(coxinla.vet2)

messages.subject_clean: Calculate DIC and WAIC manually
messages.body_plain:
To calculate DIC and WAIC the codes are as follows:
model$dic$dic
model$waic$waic

While the formula for calculating them is -2 * (log likelihood - effective number of parameters). To calculate these criterion manually the codes are as follows:

DIC = -2 * (model$mlik[2] - model.f1$dic$p.eff)
WAIC = -2 * (model$mlik[2] - model.f1$waic$p.eff

But the results are not same at all, why?

messages.subject: Re: On the weight of CPO, DIC and WAIC
messages.subject_clean: On the weight of CPO, DIC and WAIC
messages.body_plain:
these are different criteria and you can not get average of them. You should choose the comparing criterion based on your data.
DIC has been criticized for sometimes being too liberal in penalizing complexity, especially in the presence of small sample sizes.
WAIC is often considered more robust than DIC, especially for small sample sizes, and is designed to be a more accurate measure of predictive performance.

but I dont know exactly about COP, I think It is like MSE. As far as I know when considering CPO, sum(model$cpo$failure) should also be checked. Please guide me in this regard and why you have taken log of CPO?

messages.subject: How to account for spatial autocorrelation when the outcome (distance cycled) is continuous?
messages.subject_clean: How to account for spatial autocorrelation when the outcome (distance cycled) is continuous?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I am new to Bayesian inference and a bit lost trying to find the best way to model the data for one of my studies.

I am trying to predict distance cycled based on population density, recreational area density, infrastructure density, road intersection density, and average gradient (hilliness). The response variable, distance cycled (km cycled per year), is continuous and strongly skewed to the right (see histogram below). Therefore, I was considering using a Gamma regression model.

 <https://i.stack.imgur.com/WND1T.png>

However, the data is areal (aggregated for small areas within a region) and according to a Moran's I test there is spatial autocorrelation in my model. So I also need to account for spatial autocorrelation.

I have looked at the Besag-York-Mollié (BYM) model (popular in disease mapping) included in the R-INLA R package. Still, I am not sure whether it would be suitable for my continuous outcome distance cycled.

I would appreciate some help with this from those who have experience modeling areal data with a continuous dependent variable. Thank you!
